title: The Battle of the Sexes
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck open with a shout-out to Chuck's classroom visit to Midtown High School in Atlanta, then cover the 1973 Battle of the Sexes tennis match between Bobby Riggs and Billy Jean King at the Houston Astrodome. They trace the context: early-1970s women's rights momentum, the growth of open tennis, the pay gap in tennis, Billy Jean King's activism, and the founding of the Original Nine, the Virginia Slims circuit, and the WTA. They describe Riggs's gambling, his publicity stunts, and his earlier win over Margaret Court ("Mother's Day Massacre"), then the match itself (Riggs's hype, the pig gift, King's win in three straight sets, and rumors that Riggs threw the match). They close with King's later career, her outing and relationship with Marilyn Barnett, the continuing pay equity fight in tennis, and a listener mail correction about Irish nationality for Ernest Shackleton and Tom Crean.

segments.title: Opening banter and Chuck's Midtown High School visit
segments.summary: Chuck describes speaking to a junior class at Midtown High School in Atlanta about a student podcast project, and Josh and Chuck joke about the visit and a jacket.

segments.title: Introduction to the Battle of the Sexes and Bobby Riggs
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the 1973 tennis match between Bobby Riggs and Billy Jean King, note the 2017 film with Steve Carell and Emma Stone, and frame Riggs as a publicity-seeking gambler whose sexist persona may have been a gambit.

segments.title: Early 1970s context: women's rights and open tennis
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the early 1970s women's rights climate, Title IX, the Equal Rights Amendment, the growth of American tennis, and the introduction of open tournaments. They note Billy Jean King's early activism and her 1960s pay complaints.

segments.title: Tennis pay gap and Billy Jean King's early activism
segments.summary: The hosts describe prize money disparities in tennis, including the Wimbledon 1968 difference, and King's career and early feminist stance.

segments.title: Founding the Virginia Slims circuit and the Original Nine
segments.summary: King and Gladys Heldman respond to the Pacific Southwest Open's unequal purse by starting a separate tournament. The USLTA threatens suspensions, nine players sign contracts for one dollar each, and Virginia Slims sponsors the new circuit, which later merges with the USLTA.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: Formation of the Women's Tennis Association
segments.summary: In 1973 in London, women players form the WTA as a union. They threaten to boycott the US Open unless women receive equal prize money, and the US Open agrees.

segments.title: Bobby Riggs's background and gambling
segments.summary: Riggs was a top men's player in 1946 and 1947, then left the tour to hustle bets. The hosts describe his loud, provocative persona and his remarks about women, and how the challenge to King arose.

segments.title: Riggs challenges Billy Jean King
segments.summary: Riggs publicly challenges King, who declines citing her busy schedule and the risk to the women's movement if she lost.

segments.title: Margaret Court match, the Mother's Day Massacre
segments.summary: Margaret Court agrees to play Riggs in May 1973 in a match broadcast on CBS. Riggs wins 6-2, 6-1 using junk shots, after months of serious training. King watches and later decides to play him.

segments.title: Riggs's publicity stunts and insults
segments.summary: Riggs gives media interviews, makes provocative claims, presents King with roses in the Court match context, appears on Time's cover, and shows up with cut-out shirt at practice. King calls him a creep at a press conference.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Match day setup: Astrodome, audience, and odds
segments.summary: The match takes place September 20, 1973 at the Houston Astrodome with about 30,000 in person and roughly 90 million viewers. Odds favored Riggs six to one. Coverage treated the event as a sexist spectacle, and celebrities including John Wayne, Bill Cosby, and O.J. Simpson attended.

segments.title: Match production: format, entrances, and piglet gift
segments.summary: ABC earned about 1.2 million dollars from ads. The match was best of five sets, unlike the three-set women's format. King arrived on a platform carried by men in togas, and Riggs was carried by women. Riggs gave King a Sugar Daddy candy, and she gave him a piglet she named Bobby Riggs.

segments.title: Commentators and broadcast choices
segments.summary: Jack Kramer was pulled from the broadcast because of his past actions against the women's tour. Gene Scott called the match straight. Howard Cosell was brought in as commentator.

segments.title: The match result and Riggs's reaction
segments.summary: King wins in three straight sets, 6-4, 6-3, 6-3. She wore Riggs down with long rallies. Riggs took the first set 6-4 in a closer start earlier, then lost. Riggs accepted defeat graciously, hopping the net to concede. Media coverage was sentimental.

segments.title: Rumors that Riggs threw the match
segments.summary: The hosts discuss rumors that Riggs threw the match to pay gambling debts to mobsters, the 2013 ESPN report, and King's view that he lost honestly.

segments.title: Film adaptation and Battle of the Sexes culture
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 2017 film starring Steve Carell and Emma Stone, its casting and accuracy, and a related film by Yorgos Lanthimos.

segments.title: Aftermath: Riggs stunts, King's later career, and pay equity
segments.summary: Riggs tried to jump from a bridge and was stopped. King founded the Women's Sports Foundation in 1974 and publicly came out in 1981 after Marilyn Barnett's lawsuit. Ongoing tennis pay gaps include the 2024 Canadian Open figures. The hosts note King visited Riggs before his 1995 death.

segments.title: Closing remarks on the match
segments.summary: Hosts reflect on the match and mention Steve Carell and a Tim Robbins reference.

segments.title: Listener mail: Irish nationality correction
segments.summary: A listener named Efa from Ireland points out that Ernest Shackleton and Tom Crean were described as British in a prior episode, though both were born in Ireland. Chuck and Josh apologize.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to send feedback by email and the show closes with production credits.
